style_guide:
# Brand Lookbook and Visual Direction

## Design intent

Create a restrained editorial lookbook that translates a grounded brand idea into a coherent seasonal visual system and executable collection. The narrative should connect origin and values to a seasonal theme, an evidence-based consumer perspective, color and typography, product families, image direction, retail and communication touchpoints, and production milestones. Bone and oat surfaces create quiet space; taupe and stone convey tactility; rust provides one human accent; ink preserves editorial authority.

The previews define visual character and composition only. Do not copy their brand, founder, season, consumer identity, cities, quotations, garments, materials, suppliers, prices, quantities, sustainability claims, dates, typefaces, palette names, or production plan. Every factual element must come from the current workspace.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `46–60 px` side margins, `26–34 px` top framing, and a fine footer rule.
- Use a 12-column grid with `18–22 px` gutters. Align editorial titles, photography, story modules, palette swatches, product counts, captions, touchpoint cards, and production dates.
- Reserve `100–145 px` for the chapter label, expressive title, and one concise editorial sentence.
- Favor asymmetry with calm balance: portrait image beside consumer copy, story text beside material still life, title-and-range list beside paired looks, or photography beside applications and timeline.
- Use flat paper-like fields, square edges, hairline rules, and no shadow. Negative space is a core component, not leftover space.

## Color system

- Bone: `#F5F0E8` for the main canvas and lightest garments or surfaces.
- Oat: `#E8DDCD` for secondary panels and warm tonal separation.
- Sand: `#C9B79C` and taupe `#927B59` for materials, captions, and supporting range structure.
- Rust: `#A9533D` for one editorial word, selected item, chapter marker, or production decision.
- Ink: `#292620` for typography, rules, dark panels, and final hierarchy.
- Keep at least 70% of each analytical page in bone, oat, or image-neutral space. Rust should appear once or twice per composition, never as a broad promotional fill.

## Typography

- Use a high-contrast editorial serif such as `Cormorant Garamond`, `Bodoni Moda`, or `Georgia` for expressive titles and selected quotations.
- Use `Inter`, `Helvetica Neue`, `Arial`, or another neutral sans-serif for product information, specifications, schedules, and captions.
- Cover title: `54–72 px`; page title: `36–48 px`; editorial body: `13–17 px`; product and specification text: `10–13 px`; chapter metadata: `8–10 px`.
- Italics may emphasize one mood word, seasonal contrast, or product name. Do not italicize operational tables.
- Use wide tracking for chapter labels and compact tabular numerals for prices, SKU counts, dates, ratios, and production quantities.

## Components and visual language

- Story modules should connect provenance, craft, ethos, and the current seasonal implication without turning unverified history into fact.
- Consumer pages may pair one authorized portrait with behavior, wardrobe, value, and aesthetic evidence. Avoid fictional biographies masquerading as research.
- Palette pages should show named swatches, precise values, relative distribution, material implications, and accessibility or reproduction notes.
- Typography panels need font role, approved weight, size range, line spacing, licensing status, and fallback.
- Product pages should organize looks or items by family, silhouette, material, color, price, and status while preserving editorial breathing room.
- Application pages should connect visual rules to retail, print, digital, social, packaging, campaign, and production timing.
- Caption every image with status such as sample, prototype, reference, approved campaign, or final production.

## Page families

### Editorial cover

Pair a tall rights-cleared campaign or fitting image with a large stacked title on bone. Include brand, season or volume, presenter, studio, date, document status, and one sentence defining the visual-direction purpose.

### Brand story and seasonal theme

Use one tactile still life or material study between a concise brand story and a seasonal thesis panel. Translate the theme into observable choices in silhouette, material, light, behavior, and communication.

### Consumer and aesthetic keywords

Pair a verified consumer portrait or research artifact with grounded attributes and a short hierarchy of aesthetic terms. Show the evidence source and avoid reducing a broad audience to one decorative persona.

### Color, typography, and visual system

Use a horizontal palette with exact values and intended proportions, plus a compact type specimen and application rules. Include contrast, print, screen, material, and licensing considerations where relevant.

### Product collection and lifestyle

Present a small number of hero looks or product groups with clean captions and one concise range architecture. State sample or production status, material, colorway, price basis, and image provenance.

### Applications and production timeline

Combine one strong environment or retail image with four application touchpoints and a dark production schedule. Show owners, approvals, deliverables, dependencies, and final handoff rather than dates alone.

## Imagery and art direction

- Use rights-cleared or commissioned photography with soft natural light, warm neutral grading, long shadows, tactile materials, and uncluttered interiors.
- Maintain consistent crop logic: full-length product silhouette, close material study, environmental application, and quiet consumer portrait.
- Retouch naturally and preserve actual material color. Label AI-generated or composited concept imagery where used.
- Avoid trend collages, random luxury interiors, generic runway photographs, and imagery that implies an unavailable product or location.

## Content integrity and production truth

- Do not invent brand history, founder story, consumer research, quotations, collection size, garment composition, traceability, certifications, durability, repair terms, price, margin, inventory, launch timing, or retail commitments.
- Distinguish concept, reference, sketch, sample, approved design, production-ready item, final asset, and live application.
- Sustainability and provenance claims require traceable evidence, defined scope, certification status, and applicable methodology.
- Specify color-management context where exact reproduction matters: RGB, CMYK, spot, textile standard, finish, substrate, and approved sample.
- Verify font licensing, image rights, model releases, trademarks, product availability, packaging requirements, accessibility, and regional claims.
- Product counts, prices, sizes, materials, and timelines need source dates and responsible owners. Do not make a concept render appear purchasable.
- Protect personal and supplier information, unpublished designs, pricing, and production details according to the document's audience.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview brand names, consumer persona, cities, garments, palette values, typefaces, product counts, prices, applications, or dates.
- Do not use quiet-luxury styling to disguise missing strategy, unsupported provenance, or impractical production.
- Do not overfill the page, repeat a uniform card grid, or add decorative labels with no design rule behind them.
- Do not use glossy gradients, glass effects, heavy shadows, saturated rainbow palettes, fake magazine mastheads, or illegible micro-captions.
- Do not present mood imagery as final product proof or sustainability language as verified without evidence.
